Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Only the plain.

By deciding to (attempt to) cancel the whole current block window and replace it
with a new one (the new block window resulting from the alteration of the
target), one is clearly deciding not to (attempt to) block in the current window
(the window one is attempting to cancel).

Wow. None of the half-dozen or so playgroups I've played with have
gotten this rule correct, apparently.

Here's what I don't understand about what you wrote above: why does
_attempting_ to cancel the current block window _actually_ cancel the
current block window? It seems extremely counter-intuitive to me to
have the block window cancelled if the bounce card is also cancelled -
the effect that would close the block window never occurred, so why
does the window close anyway? I don't see why playing an effect which

The rules are pretty clear that the phases of a turn go in a particular
order and don't go backwards. By normal rules, you can play reactions
before and after declining to block. There's no text on deflection that
limits it to being played after declining to block.

Sure, if deflection has been successfully played, then you've lost your
opportunity to block because the target has changed, creating a new
block window and closing the old one. But there's no rule (or card text
on deflection) that states that your block window closes when you
_attempt_ to play a card that would close that window if it were
successfully played, and that you still close that window when the card
is canceled.

I mean, if played a master that said "End your master phase..." and it
got Washed, I'd expect that I'd get to stay in my master phase, unless
it had explicit text that said "... even if this card is canceled".

The rulebook says that Minions can only attempt actions during the
Minion Phase. Clearly if they played an Action Card, they were in
either the Cheat Phase or the Minion Phase. Neither the Rulebook nor
Deflection says Deflection "can only be played if the reacting minion's
controller has chosen not to block". 6.2.2 states "Once a Methuselah
decides not to make any further attempts to block, that decision is
final." You've time and again supported the idea that Block Forfeiture
needs to be explicitly declared.

I'm with Johannes in being confused on this one. (I thought there was even a
semi-recent thread about this topic, but I couldn't immediately find it.)

Assume the following:

SCENARIO 1

Meths: A > B > C

Meth A: Frederick the Weak bleeds with Legal Manipulation.
Meth B: No block.
Meth A: Frederick plays Aire of Elation.
Meth B (who controls exactly 1 untapped vampire with DOM): Keith Moody plays
SUP Deflection to bounce to Meth C.
Meth C: I play Direct Intervention on the Deflection. (The DI is not
Suddened or Washed.)
Meth B has no Redirection and so must take the bleed, since she declined to
block.

SCENARIO 2

Meths: A > B > C

Meth A: Frederick the Weak bleeds with Legal Manipulations.
Meth B: [SILENCE]
Meth A: Frederick plays Aire of Elation.
Meth B: Keith Moody plays SUP Deflection to bounce to Meth C.
Meth C: I play Direct Intervention on the Deflection. (The DI is not
Suddened.)
Meth B still has no Redirection and but has the option to block, since she
did not decline to do so.

I was remembering that scenario 1 is different from scenario 2 because of
the absence of a "no block" declaration.

The original quoted ruling:

http://groups.google.be/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/f4e7d18691d047b3?dmode=source&hl=nl

"Declaring that one is not blocking is implicit in playing Deflection
(unlike playing Telepathic Counter). [LSJ 30-AUG-1999]

would seem to equate the two scenarios.

(There is also SCENARIO 3, where Meth A forces Meth B to declare whether she
is blocking before playing the Aire. Scenario 3 seems to be the preferred
approach by the World-Wide Player A Association, but I'm assuming that
Player A doesn't belong to the WWPAA.)

- Pat

It kind of sounds like what LSJ is saying is that it isn't _legal_ to play
a bleed retargeter while your block window is still open. Therefore, to
even play the block retargerter at all, you must have volunteered to close
your block window. Then, if the retargeter gets canceled by whatever means,
you're not allowed to back up and reopen the block window.

your block window is open doesn't seem very well documented.

> >> your block window. Then, if the retargeter gets canceled by whatever means,
> >> you're not allowed to back up and reopen the block window.
> >

> > action) I am implicitly declining to play any further action modifiers
> > during the current action, so if my Kiss of Ra gets DI'ed I cannot back
> > up and play action modifiers?
>
> I don't think so. I think you're just trying to play Kiss of Ra.

No, no. According to Scott's reasoning playing cards implies that you
have made decisions, so playing Kiss of Ra implies you have no
intention to play any more action modifiers (i.e., you are closing the
window where action modifiers can be played during an action, because
you are endind that action).

> I'm saying
> that if a bleed retargeter is not legal to play until your block window was
> closed by your voluntarily closing it, then LSJ's logic makes sense. And it
> makes his comparison to the closing of the untap window by playing a Giant's
> Blood make some sense. But I admit, I didn't know the block window was a
> phase that had to be closed before someone could play a bleed retargeter.

When a card gets cancelled, it does not take effect. So you are not
actually redirecting a bleed action by the time you play Deflection,
since there is a previous "window" where as-the-card-is-played effects
can be played before Deflection's card text applies.

> I don't think your comparison to Kiss of Ra is correct either way, though.
> Playing an action modifier couldn't possibly be illegal during the time
> it's legal to play action modifiers - that's self-contradictory.

The fact is that, as others have already pointed out, there are no such
windows in the rulebook, and that Deflection's card text does not say
anything about closing your block window. So Scott's ruling is counter
intuitive (although his logic makes sense).

My 2 cents, for what it's worth

When you announce the action "I'm going to bleed you for X" you ask
your prey (assuming no kindred spirits/night moves) are you going to
block (NOT are you going to redirect the bleed), if they say no, you
then ask if anyone else wishes to block (via eagles sight or Anneke).
After this the block window on the action is closed.

After all attempts to block the action are settled, your prey can then
react with redirect or reduce. If you reduce the bleed one of 2 things
will happen, the bleed will resovle for a lesser amount or you can
still redirect the reduced bleed if you wish. If the bleed is
redirected at this stage (or immediatly after the block window closes
more likely) the Methusalah who is the new target once more has the
option to block (and I would assume Anneke and eagles sight once more
become viable block techniques) This continues to occour until the
action is successful (even for 0) or is blocked, I.E. resolved.

Although this is not spelled out directly in the rules the way in which
the rules are written and sequenced strongly suggest that this is the
way they are intended to function. Is it counter-intuiative? maybe, but

I don't think so.

Sutekh_23

If the player who incorrectly pitched away his pool was trying to see
if the opponent was going to play a modifier and then back up and
declare a block, he's broken the rules. If he did so intentionally,
he's cheating (and there are guidelines for how a judge should handle
that), and if he wasn't cheating (maybe because he thought it was legal
play), then he should still not be allowed to use any knowledge gleaned
to his advantage (as far as I understand it).

It seems to me that the best way to handle it is _typically_ to rewind
the game state to the point just after the target has declined to block
and allow the acting minion to play cards. But this is what we have
judges for.

It is better for the steps in the game to be explicit and separate from each
other than for them to be implicit and bound inextricably together. It
makes for a clearer and more consistent rules set. That's why people here
appear to find it more intuitive that declining to block should be separate
from whether or not a Deflection is played.

> Why should canceling your Bewitching Oration not also cancel your implied
> "I don't play Bribes"?

That's another example of card plays that occur in defined separate steps of
the game. It's not a relevant comparison to Deflection versus the decision
whether to attempt a block.

Rulebook [6.2] Taking an Action: "Note that action modifiers and reaction
cards can be played at any time in this process as appropriate, subject to
the restrictions on adding stealth and intercept listed below and the
restrictions against the same minion playing the same action modifier or
reaction card more than once (see "Minion Cards," sec. 1.6.3), and following
the same sequencing strictures of all effects (see "Sequencing," sec.
1.6.1.6)."

Deflection doesn't have any inherent restrictions on when it can be played;
therefore, it ought logically to be playable at any point in the course of a
bleed action, including before deciding whether to attempt to block.

Messages.Author: witness1
Messages.Body:
XZealot wrote:

> LSJ wrote:
> > If you're trying to communicate ("flesh out in the mind") that you're not
> > blocking in order to draw out the modifier that the acting Methuselah intends to
> > play after you decline to block, then your communication of "no block" counts as
> > your declaration of "no block".
> >
> > You can always bounce after a modifier, of course.
>
> How is the action any more or less resolved if you can play a bounce
> but can't announce a block if you haven't declined to block"?

The 'your communication of "no block"' means that you have declined to
block, even if you didn't use the English language to convey that
message.

> If the action isn't completed by the obvious playing of an action
> modifier then why are you disallowed from blocking?

Because you declined to block. Y'know, because you aren't just throwing
your pool into the blood bank for kicks.

> If the acting player can wait until you have pitched a pool to announce
> his action modifier then why can't a player who has not been asked "Do
> you block?" not try and block?

You have sped past several steps in the action sequence by pitching
that pool, only some of which you have control over. You have sped past
the "I decline to block" step, impicitly declaring as you did so that
you did not wish to block. That's legal, because you're allowed to
decide for yourself if you want to block or not. You have also sped
past the "allow acting minion to play further modifiers". That's the
illegal part, because you haven't allowed the other player the option
to play his cards. That's where you should rewind to.

> It seems remarkably parallel to me.

It's not. If you speed past your own option to play a card or effect,
you lose your window (see also, gaining pool for the edge). If you
speed past someone else's opportunity to play effects, then you don't
rewind all the way to the start of the phase, you rewind to window that
you illegally sped through.

Similarly, if someone had a Madness Network in play and you started
your transfers without allowing him to take actions, you should rewind
and let him take actions, but not (generally) rewind far enough to
allow you to take more actions first (you implicitly declared that you
were done with actions by moving on to influence).

Messages.Author: CthuluKitty
Messages.Body:
The weird inconsistency I'm seeing with this ruling is that it causes a
step in the timing sequence to be skipped. At present a minion can
play Deflection before the player explicitly states that he is not
blocking. If the play of Deflection automatically implies the latter,
then two things are happening at once. Under all other circumstances,
the declination to block passes priority to the acting player. This
ruling on bounce cards causes that window to be skipped, as the
reacting player simultaneously declines to block and plays a reaction,
without giving the acting player a chance to play action modifiers. At
present there are no cards in the game that would care if they were
played in this window, but the timing issue is very bizarre.

Ultimately this would seem to require an actual text modification of
all four bounce effects to say that they cannot be played until after
blocks have been declined, or else there's a gaping exception in the
timing rules. This whole affair strikes me not so much as a ruling,
but as a change to card text.

No, the parallel I was denying was the analogy, not the ruling. You gave a
number of analogies over the course of this discussion, all of which
appeared to be intended to *show* that the ruling that playing Deflection =
"I already declined to block" made sense, but they only worked as analogies
if one already *accepted* that playing Deflection = "I already declined to
block".

Sure, as you say, a ruling can exist simply by fiat. But normally (IMO)
there should be some good logic and reasons behind it. A ruling that exists
only by fiat, and would be better the other way, is not a good ruling.

> Unless you have the ruling as it is: that the Deflection case is also an
> example of a card play that occurs in a defined separate step of the game
> (after the
> "I don't block" declaration).

Except that there's no reason for that ruling to exist, as far as I can see.
Nor have you provided such a reason, as yet. Nor is there card-text on
Deflection making it so, nor, as Greg and Bram have pointed out, would it be
a worthwhile project to add such card-text to make it so, since the effect
is unnecessary and therefore undesirable to add to the game.

As far as I can discover through Google-groups, the idea arose on August 30,
1999, that Deflection implicitly required you to have made a decision not to
block, in a description of when you would burn blood for failing to block
for Forced Awakening. I don't know why this implicit "obviously I'm not
blocking because now I'm not the target anymore" side-effect of Deflection
should be such a big deal, and apparently neither did you when you answered
a different post on December 6, 2001, saying that Deflection could be played
and canceled with Direct Intervention before the decision to decline blocks
had been made.

There has been presented no motivation for why Deflection should now have to
appear after (or create) the "I don't block" step of the game. There has
been no reason presented that the description of how Deflection operated
once upon a time in an interaction with Forced Awakening (for all of two
days!) should stand, but the description of how Deflection interacted once
upon a time with Faceless Night should not.

There's just no apparent reason for this ruling to exist and require putting
new card text on the bleed-bounce cards that we've had for twelve years.
Unless you know of some such reason, it seems to me that leaving the
bleed-bounce texts as they are and dropping the ruling would be the far
better course of action.

Josh

After reading your replies, it's still not clear to me why the attempt
of changing the target, would imply denial to block. I would appreciate
it if you could help me clear things up :)

strictly cardtext, this is not explicitly stated, right? Nowhere does
it say: "You can only change the target of a bleed, or play a card that
does so after declaring wether or not you attempt to block" or
similarily "Playing a card that can change the target of a bleed means
you deny to block" nor "to attempt to open a new blocking window, there
may not be a current one"

Your argument is based on, correct me if I'm wrong:

If the target of a bleed changes, a new blocking window is opened.
Therefore: If you *attempt* to change the target of a bleed, you are
implicitly closing the current blocking window to allow for the next
one to be opened.

into play?

be true: "when the target of a bleed (or any directed action) is
(successfully) changed, the current blocking window is closed, and a
new one opened."

Could you clarify your reasoning why you feel the attempt per se
(playing the card - instead of it successfully resolving) closes the
blocking window? To me it seems incongruous with the explicit rules or
cardtext.

Thanks in advance,
B

> The basis is: if you are attempting to close the window without blocking, then
> it is true that you are declining to block in that
> to-be-closed-without-you-blocking window.

If attempting to make me unable to block means I decline to block,

*Determine - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block
*Direct Intervention - if cancelled (and I was DIing an action card), I
cannot attempt to block
*Mistaken Identity - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block
*The Mole [dom] - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block
*Rewind Time [tem] - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block
*Scry the Hearthstone [VIS] - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block
*Unseen Hibernation [abo/ABO] - if cancelled, I cannot attempt to block

If attempting to make me unable to vote means I decline to vote,
*Delaying Tactics - if cancelled, I (and my minions) cannot vote
*Direct Intervention - if cancelled (and I was DIing a political action
or Delaying Tactics or a card that would render a political action
blocked), I (and my minions) cannot vote

If attempting to make me unable to act in a given phase of combat means
I decline to act in that phase of combat...

Do you want to see how far down this rabbit hole goes?

*IF MY ATTEMPT IS SUCCESSFUL* (emphasis added :), I will be unable to
block. That's what we call contingency. You don't forfeit your main
plan just because you have a contingency. I'm not declining to block by
playing Deflection, I'm doing something orthogonal to blocking. I'm not
trying to close the blocking window, I'm trying to change the nature of
the window.

--
- Gregory Stuart Pettigrew

Messages.Body:

news:d4Ufh.23014$9v5....@newssvr29.news.prodigy.net...


That fact isn't really related to the "attempting to play Deflection means
you have already declined to block" ruling though. Only appropriate effects
are allowed during an action; when a block attempt is declared, if the
acting minion passes on adding stealth, the block succeeds and only effects
that are legal on a successful block (e.g. Obedience) can be played.
Whether attempting to play Deflection means that you have already declined
to block is only relevant in that, if you are currently succeeding in
blocking, you can't play Deflection (just as you can't play Precognition).

Josh

No matter how many times I read it or quote it, it has yet to become more of
an established fact. :-)

It is still the outcome of your "clarification" and not an a priori obvious
fact of the world (to anyone but you).

It makes more sense to everyone else to say that it is true that, after you
have *succeeded* in closing the window of your possibility to block by
changing the target of the action, you have *then* declined to block in your
normal blocking window.

>> It is at least as sensible (of course, I would say more sensible) that
>> you may wish to *continue* your (currently failing) block attempt if you
>> *attempt* to change the target of the bleed but fail to actually change
>> the bleed's target.
>
> What current block attempt?

The one that Anson is attempting to make against Ozmo's bleed. But Ozmo
adds stealth, so his block is no longer succeeding. So he tries to Deflect
the bleed, but the Deflection is canceled with Direct Intervention. So he
would like to continue his block attempt, but unfortunately you've told him
that he can't, because his window closed when he tried to change the target.
I guess he should have known better. Do, or do not, there is no try.

This is why your ruling doesn't seem sensible to me. It seems illogical
that your vampire can be trying to block, fail to currently block, then try
to Deflect, have the Deflection canceled, and then be unable to resume
attempting to block. Since the target never actually changed (see
Banishment vs Diamond Thunderbolt for a similar "change never occurred"
situation), it seems only natural that the original (and only) target would
still be able to try to block.

Josh

it would if playing Deflection actually closed the window.

but it doesn't.

the player closes the window by declining to block, and then they are
allowed to play deflection. it's just that if they skip the bit where
they close the window and move straight on to playing deflection, then
all players (and the game state) assume that they have closed the window
prior to the play, else they couldn't have played the deflection in the
first place.[0]

I don't actually like the ruling, but it does hold up to scrutiny if the
axiom, that you must close the blocking window before you can even
attempt to open a new one elsewhere, holds.

If this axiom did not hold, you'd be able to play Deflection during a
block attempt. I'd like to unaxiate (I am sure that's a word. shut up),
this one, and have a new axiom that allowed you to play deflection
before or after block attempts, but not during. I don't know how you'd
phrase it, technically (maybe in the way i just did, as a ruling?), but
it would then align the rules to the way people actually play.

[0] Parallel, as stated elsewhere, to ditching pool for a bleed without
explicitly declining to block. It implies you have declined to block.



True. It seems illogical that the initial blocker can't re-attempt to
block ("If one attempt to block fails, another can be made as often as
the blocking Methuselah wishes", 6.2.2.1 rulebook) after failing to
change the target of the bleed. After all, the target never changed.
The original blocking Methuselah is still the same blocking Methuselah.

but is currently not succeeding (not enough intercept vs stealth),
general-case effects are legal. It is possible to gain intercept at
this point by playing a card of your own; it is possible for someone
else to give intercept to you whether you want it or not (e.g. by
London Evening Star); it is possible for you to reduce the bleed amount
with Telepathic Counter; it is possible for you to attempt to change
the target of the bleed with Deflection. In all of these cases except,
according to you, the attempt to change the target of the bleed, it is
obviously still legal to renew (or continue, take your pick) your
would-be blocker's efforts to block after playing those other effects
(even if the other effects have no benefit to the blocker's ability to
block). I don't see any logical reason why Deflection should be so
different and, even when canceled and *not* changing the target of the
bleed, have the unexpected effect of still requiring an irreversible
declination of blocking.

Josh

Messages.Author: rdco...@gmail.com

> I don't like the idea that minion cards can be cancelled by master
> cards. The success or otherwise of minion actions should be resolved by
> the interaction between minions and not be influenced by the direct
> intervention of the methusalehs.

There's a little trilogy of masters that kind of go together in this
aspect, for my money:

Sudden Reversal
Direct Intervention
Personal Involvement

Sudden reversal has the virtue of being a master card that cancels
master cards (like for like), and when introduced (jyhad) was the sole
defense against master cards being played.

Personal Involvement kind of has the virtue of requirement and caveat,
but in principle I think it was a poor design decision, for the "direct
methuselah action" reason, I particularly dislike it in that it is such
direct and transient offensive action from a master card.

Direct Intervention lacks the like for like concept, lacks the "sole
defense" requirement, and has nary a caveat nor requirement to reign it
in. Its only vague step back from being utterly unreasonable is that
its an out of turn master; meaning that its only "offensive" use is in
cross-table meddling (though it would make a great tool for
collusion...), which is somewhat scant virtue, IMO.

To me its quite clear that the art for DI should really have been a
nice bullet surrounded by little sparkles of magicalness, its flavour
text: "better than penicillin, baby"

scenario to encompass only that which proves your point. The reality of
the situation is that action modifiers may be played before block
attempts are made. You conveniently left that out of your scenario
above.

For example, you have specifically ruled that a player may play a
Conditioning on an action before the defender, who just so happens to
have a Blessings of Chaos which would prevent the acting player from
being able to do so, may declare a block.

So in your own rulings you have stated that action modifiers that
modify the amount of the bleed can be played before block attempts are
declared.

So it is, in fact, more complicated than the scenario you laid down is.

A) action is announced
B) Action modifiers are played
C) Reactions are played
D) Block attempts are declared
E) Action Modifiers are played
F) Reactions are played
G) Combat ensues from a successful block.
H) If blocking minion fails, then other block attempts are solicited.
I) Barring another minion successfully blocking
1) You decline to block
2) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to block
3) The acting Methuselah declines to play modifiers
4) You decline to play reactions
5) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to play reactions
6) You pitch a pool into the bank

Now what constitutes resolution of the action? It is in fact an
agreement between players that the action is resolved and no other
effects are in play. This is why ruling that pitching a pool is an
automatic block decline is anti-thetical to the basic nature of VTES.

Pitching a pool is fundamental to the aquiecence that the action is
resolved. When the acting player plays an action modifier it
fundamentally represents a disagreement between the players that the
action is not resolved. This would then reset the chain of interaction
to a point agreed upon by the players involved.

The most fair point to reset it is to point B not to point 3. As
players can agree that everything that follows point B has not been
resolved.
_________________
Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr
XZealot
Archon of the Swamp

> can cancel something like 80% of the cards in print, rather than a
> more-specialized minion card with narrower effects. For the most part VTES
> is built around minion cards and most of them have requirements to play.

"For the most part" != "all the time". There are other master cards which are
uncharacteristically broad. Ascendance is a no-requirements card that just
hands you a pool, for instance, without regard to whether you have any vampires
or any permanents at all. Sudden Reversal is a very comparable no-requirements
master card which cancels master cards and Not To Be is a no-requirements
master card which cancels event cards, and so forth. The 80% thing is
interesting, I suppose, but ultimately not an argument by itself.

> For the most part, it is not built around such broad general effects.

I don't think you can make such a broad, general statement. Taste, of course,
is reasonable enough argument for liking or not liking a given card - as far
as it goes. But uniqueness of a particular game component is not. Any
card game which has one and only one wild card (e.g. some Hoyle deck card game
in which only the jokers are wild) is a counterexample to such logic. Chess
has one and only one king, a piece that must always be defended at peril of
game loss as opposed to all the other pieces which may be readily sacrificed.
And it works quite well, I'm told.

> That's what I assume Jeroen means when he says Direct Intervention doesn't
> really fit the game. It's a very out-of-character card design for the game
> of VTES.

It's somewhat out of character, I'll grant you. But that by itself doesn't
make it bad. The assertion needs more justification behind it for a reader
to decide whether he can agree with it or not. Otherwise it has to be judged
baseless.

Fred

The bits of the action that went before the pause in which you pitch a pool were
not listed, as they are not relevant, yes.

At the pause (a "pass" from the acting Methuselah, awaiting a reaction or a
block attempt or a declaration of "no block" from you, the target), which occurs

> agreement between players that the action is resolved and no other
> effects are in play.

Yes.

You show that agreement (your part and the part you assume on others) by
pitching in a pool.

And the first step of that agreement, by the rules, is your declination to block.

If, after making that first step, the acting Methuselah declines to modify,
fine. But if she does not, but rather chooses to play a Conditioning, well,
that's her prerogative. Doing so won't cause the state to rewind to the point
before your declination.

Agreement is not simultaneous. It is a sequence, as prescribed by the rulebook.

I personally see DI as much worse for the game than PTO. PTO, even though
powerful, is just one specific type of card and you can see it coming from
miles away -- it only works in specific types of decks. DI is unique as a
general-use, minimal-restrictions trump card that can (and often does) go
in each and every deck, in multiple copies. There's a vast difference.

//Petri

you know, formal play needs formally defined rules.

>>> sure what you could mean by a card "fitting the game" anyway. Direct
>>> Interventions are two and a half by four inches, just like all the other
>>> cards. They totally fit the game.
>>
>> It doesn't fit the game in that it's a master card with no requirements
>> that
>> can cancel something like 80% of the cards in print, rather than a
>> more-specialized minion card with narrower effects. For the most part
>> VTES
>> is built around minion cards and most of them have requirements to play.
>
> "For the most part" != "all the time".

Well of course!

> There are other master cards which are
> uncharacteristically broad. Ascendance is a no-requirements card that
> just
> hands you a pool, for instance, without regard to whether you have any
> vampires
> or any permanents at all. Sudden Reversal is a very comparable
> no-requirements
> master card which cancels master cards and Not To Be is a no-requirements
> master card which cancels event cards, and so forth. The 80% thing is
> interesting, I suppose, but ultimately not an argument by itself.

Your comparisons don't exemplify the same kind of broadness. Being playable
all the time without requirements (Ascendance) is not the same as "affecting
a vast swath of other cards" (Direct Intervention). Nor is "being playable
against a smaller set of cards" (Sudden Reversal, Not To Be) the same as
"being playable against the largest set of cards in the game". As Jeroen
pointed out, the fact that DI is usable against 74.3% of the game's printed
library cards is exactly the point. There are 30 Event cards, 3
Convictions, and 406 masters, versus 1269 different minion cards in my ARDB
file. And the usual deckbuilding rules of thumb put no more than 20% master
cards into any given VTES deck (often less). The fact that Direct
Intervention is able to cancel *any* of those is a very large window of
applicability. Far more than other cards that can cancel much smaller
subsets of the cardpool - e.g. Iron Heart, which is only able to cancel 27
different Presence or Dominate cards.

>> For the most part, it is not built around such broad general effects.
>
> I don't think you can make such a broad, general statement.

heh! I think I can! Are there a lot of other similarly broad and general
effects you can use in VTES? Not that I can see.

> Taste, of course,
> is reasonable enough argument for liking or not liking a given card - as
> far
> as it goes. But uniqueness of a particular game component is not. Any
> card game which has one and only one wild card (e.g. some Hoyle deck card
> game
> in which only the jokers are wild) is a counterexample to such logic.
> Chess
> has one and only one king, a piece that must always be defended at peril
> of
> game loss as opposed to all the other pieces which may be readily
> sacrificed.
> And it works quite well, I'm told.

The game of VTES was built without Direct Intervention; DI was added later,
in the Sabbat expansion. If you look at the game as a whole, and the
evolution of the game over time, I think it's clear that the game was not
built on broad, general effects, but on small, narrow effects. It's the
adding up of many such small and narrow effects that normally accomplishes
things in VTES. That's why Direct Intervention is outside the normal
paradigm. I agree that the fact there's only one card named Direct
Intervention isn't the point - its *effect* is the point.

>> That's what I assume Jeroen means when he says Direct Intervention
>> doesn't
>> really fit the game. It's a very out-of-character card design for the
>> game
>> of VTES.
>
> It's somewhat out of character, I'll grant you. But that by itself
> doesn't
> make it bad. The assertion needs more justification behind it for a
> reader
> to decide whether he can agree with it or not. Otherwise it has to be
> judged
> baseless.

Uh... the justification was right there. Out of character -> doesn't really
fit the game. That is, an out of character card design isn't in-character
with the game as a whole, which is pretty much what it means to "not really
fit the game".

That doesn't necessarily mean it's *bad*, no, but I wasn't necessarily
describing it as *bad*. I was describing it as being out of character for
the game.

Hopefully that clarifies what I'm trying to say a little? This turned into
a kind of rambly post as I wrote it... :-)

Josh

I believe the difference here is that the play was incorrect because it
encapsulated multiple steps, some of which rightfully belong to other
players (and are therefore illegal for this player). So (without using
details), I do X, which encapsulates steps 1-6. Only steps 1 and 6 of
that sequence actually belong to me though, so my play was illegal.

The ruling says that the fix is to break apart the encapsulated steps,
and unwind through all the illegal steps. So steps 2-6 are undone, but
step 1 remains "done".

The alternative is to leave all of the encapsulated steps encapsulated,
and undo them as a block. While nicer to the casual player who
innocently erred, it is more open to abuse, as more sophisticated
players can use it to "fish" for information they shouldn't have when
making their step 1 decision. So declining to block and prematurely
pitching a blood in is corrected by unwinding it so that the block is
still declined.

Pitching a pool follows the resolution of a bleed for 1. Any
interuption in that resolution resets the action to the earliest
possible moment that the interuption could occur.

> > You then have specifically constructed a contrived
> > scenario to encompass only that which proves your point. The reality of

It has huge bearing. It eliminates the earlier steps in the action
that play reverts.

> > For example, you have specifically ruled that a player may play a
> > Conditioning on an action before the defender, who just so happens to
> > have a Blessings of Chaos which would prevent the acting player from
> > being able to do so, may declare a block.
>
> This is true. And irrelevant.

Actually it is relevant. This ruling benchmarks the earliest point in
an action that a action modifier may play, and therefore marks the
point to which an action reverts when a player plays an action modifier
after a defending player has "pitched a pool".

> > So in your own rulings you have stated that action modifiers that
> > modify the amount of the bleed can be played before block attempts are
> > declared.
>
> Still true.

....and incredibly relavent.

> > So it is, in fact, more complicated than the scenario you laid down is.
> >
> > A) action is announced
> > B) Action modifiers are played
> > C) Reactions are played
> > D) Block attempts are declared
> > E) Action Modifiers are played
> > F) Reactions are played
> > G) Combat ensues from a successful block.
> > H) If blocking minion fails, then other block attempts are solicited.
> > I) Barring another minion successfully blocking
> > 1) You decline to block
> > 2) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to block
> > 3) The acting Methuselah declines to play modifiers
> > 4) You decline to play reactions
> > 5) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to play reactions
> > 6) You pitch a pool into the bank
>
> This is missing the point.

No it is not missing the point. This is how actions resolve and the
various non-combat steps which are skipped/omitted on every single
action. When there is a misplay (i.e. a player pitching a pool) the
play reverts to the earliest possible step not the latest.

> The bits of the action that went before the pause in which you pitch a pool were
> not listed, as they are not relevant, yes.
>
> At the pause (a "pass" from the acting Methuselah, awaiting a reaction or a
> block attempt or a declaration of "no block" from you, the target), which occurs
> between steps I and 1 above, you pitched a pool.
>
> By doing so, you express, implicitly, steps 1 through 6 above. Of those, the
> continuous parts you actually have control of ends right after step 1. So step 1
> is the only one you force to happen. You cannot force others to skip their steps.

Incorrect, by pitching a pool without declaring a no block attempt you
are agreeing to resolve the action in its current state. When the
acting player plays an action modifier it becomes a misplay and play
rewinds to the earliest possible point. Since the reacting player has
not explicitly declared a "no block", it rewinds to step B not step 3.

> > Now what constitutes resolution of the action? It is in fact an
> > agreement between players that the action is resolved and no other
> > effects are in play.
>
> Yes.
>
> You show that agreement (your part and the part you assume on others) by
> pitching in a pool.
> And the first step of that agreement, by the rules, is your declination to block.
>
> If, after making that first step, the acting Methuselah declines to modify,
> fine. But if she does not, but rather chooses to play a Conditioning, well,
> that's her prerogative. Doing so won't cause the state to rewind to the point
> before your declination.

If a player plays an action modifier on a action that has resolved
(i.e. pool has been lost), then it is a misplay. Play is at that point
rewound to the earliest point that both players can agree upon (i.e.
step B in a situation where there is an absence of a "no block"
declaration), or barring that the misplay is disallowed (i.e. the
acting player can not play the action modifier).

> > This is why ruling that pitching a pool is an
> > automatic block decline is anti-thetical to the basic nature of VTES.
>
> > Pitching a pool is fundamental to the aquiecence that the action is
> > resolved. When the acting player plays an action modifier it
> > fundamentally represents a disagreement between the players that the
> > action is not resolved. This would then reset the chain of interaction
> > to a point agreed upon by the players involved.
>
> Correct. To step 2, above.

To step B as per the misplay guidelines.

> > The most fair point to reset it is to point B not to point 3. As
> > players can agree that everything that follows point B has not been
> > resolved.
>
> Agreement is not simultaneous. It is a sequence, as prescribed by the rulebook.

Agreement by definition is simultaneous. Both player do it at the same
time otherwise agreement does not occur. That is the nature of the
word.

This is not a point or counter-point to anything that has been said,
rather an observation:

It might be that some players extrapolate the rules governing card play
into this situation. In many facets of the game, card play goes back
and forth until one player declares they have no further plays to make.
Pitching in the Pool for the bleed of 1 is an acceptance of that
bleed, but the play of the action mod to increase it triggers the
conditioned 'option returns to me' behavior. While it is incorrect, it
might be the cause in some cases.

When one considers a different action modifier, like Freak Drive, the
absurdity becomes self evident:

MethA: Fatima bleeds for 1.
MethB: [Pitches Pool]
MethA: Fatima will Freak Drive
MethB: In that case, I'll block the action.

The only difference is the effect of the action mod, but intuition in
the case of FD is that a block attempt would not be possible at the
time of it's playing, due largely to the qualifier text on it. Putting
such text ("only usable after all block attempts have failed or been
declined") on bleed mods would be cumbersome and limiting (I would
think the intent is that they can be played as the action is announced
if desired).

What some players seem to be forgetting is that you either block or
don't after the action is declared, much like you must decide whether
or not to block a Political Action before terms are officially declared
(though they are often discussed while the threat of a block exsists).
The onus should not be on the acting player to call for block attempts,
though it is a good habit to acquire. Still, some players will simply
pitch the Pool before the acting meth can finish the declaration of the
action, because they believe that they can still block if they see a
mod they don't like.

Acting Methuselah: I attempt to bleed you with Govern the Unaligned.
Oh, and I play Seduction on Isabel de Leon.
Methuselah being bled: Hmmm. Okay. I attempt to block with Colin
Flynn.

No-one objects, even though no explicit "Do you block?" has been asked.

Consider another example in the rulebook:

Sarah announces that Ira is hunting and taps Ira. The action is
undirected and has a default of +1 stealth. Her prey declines to
block. Her predator, however, plays a reaction card to give +1
intercept to one of her ready untapped minions, Eugenio. Sarah
has no cards to play to increase Ira's stealth, so the action is
blocked. Eugenio is tapped, and combat begins.

The prey declines to block, but the evil rulebook writers have skipped
the "Do you block?" event. OH NOES. END OF TEH WORLD.

This is much like the prey declining to block by pitching a pool when
being bled.

>
> Then obviously the acting player has the ability to ask, "Do you
> block?" even after the pool has been pitched.

Pointlessly, since the question has already been answered (the defending player
cannot expect to reach the pitching pool stage unless he has declined to block;
since it was the defending player's impulse (his turn in sequence to play the
next effect), his options were: "so-and-so plays a reaction", "I play a master:
out-of-turn", "so-an-so blocks", or "no block". That is the exhaustive list of
his choices at his impulse. Which of those choices is indicated by pitching a
pool? The "no block" one, of course).

> acting player from asking, "Do you block?"

Nothing is stopping him from asking "is it my turn?" either, but both are obvious.

> Even in the rulebook it states that this is an "event".

Correct. At the defending player's impulse, though, he declined to react or
block, so it must be the case that he declined to block.

Nothing was skipped. (And it is now the acting player's impulse, since "no
block" is an event, so he may play bleed boosters).

Messages.Author: epoch_ellipse

I've only played VTES about 30 times. The first 5 times were back when
it was still called Jyhad, and the last 20 were in the last couple of
months. On one hand, this means that I don't really know what I'm
talking about. On the other hand, this might mean that I can be more
objective than the players that have been burned by the cards and
combinations of cards discussed. Maybe. I'm grateful to the Los
Angeles playgroup for encouraging me even though almost every game I'm
in times out because i have to read every card and ask what the hell
just happened. They've been very good about formally going through
every step of play so that I don't get lost. However, I can see the
value of saying "hands for one?" to save time, with the mutual
understanding that if either player wants to formally go through all
the steps of combat, it will happen. I can even see the value of
pitching one pool, but only as a non-verbal statement of the pitcher's
declination to block. Otherwise, that seems to me weasley and
disrespectful to the game and to the other players. Though I've only
seen DI played once or twice, I don't like the idea of it because it
seems to violate the spirit of the relationship between meths and
minions. I thought the meths were supposed to be so removed from the
details that minions even doubted the existence of meths. i thought
that minions were generally supposed to believe that they were working
only to advance their own agendas, or those of their clans and cohorts.
I would hate for my little minion brawls to be broken up by someone
that isn't supposed to get her hands dirty. But as for the effect the
card has on actual game play, having someone drop a DI on me isn't any
worse than someone playing Immortal Grapple when all i want to do is
end combat. The cost may seem a little low, but it does burn a pool
and a master phase action, and takes up a master card slot in the deck.
Also, in my mind it doesn't matter how often the situation comes up,
it should still be addressed.

Those are just my thoughts, now i'll bring up something related to the
original topic that i haven't seen in this thread. It's also about the
spirit of the game, and also kind of about the underlying storyline
social mechanics. The ability of any untapped ready minion controlled
by the target meth to attempt to block a bleed individually and in any
order is important to the game dynamics. It's one of the things that
IMO makes VTES a much more interesting game than MtG. The 1999 ruling
means that one minion's attempt to change the course of events strips
away the other ready untapped minions' right to do the same in ways
that they are capable of. I don't think that a minion that tries and
fails to change anything should (in this one specific case but not in
other reaction card cases) be able to screw the other ready untapped
minions out of opportunities like that. I would buy into Archon
Investigation having this effect, because it's a master card. If
anyone should be able to supercede the individual urges of a pack of
minions it should be the meth that they serve. I've tried to follow
LSJ's rebuttals, but I don't understand the logic behind the ruling to
begin with. At this time 6.2 does state that a reaction card can be
played at any time during an action, and there is nothing on Deflection
that states that it can not be played after the Announce the Action
stage but before the first part of the Resolve Any Block Attempts stage
(where i believe the blocking window lives and dies). I agree that a
block attempt should be resolved without a Deflection popping up in the
middle, because that's messy and all stages of play should be as
clearly defined and as focused as possible. I think that any
interruptions should be germaine to the situation that's unfolding at
the time. I respect LSJ's authority and I know that changes are coming
to integrate the 1999 ruling. I commend him because he's spent a lot
of time on this thread and he's doing the right thing by following the
established process to clarify the rules as questions come up. But
that doesn't explain the rationale for the ruling in the first place.
LSJ's position doesn't appear, to some on this thread (me included), to
be based on the rules or the card. I've seen LSJ state that players'
reasons for wanting to be able to attempt to block after a failed
Deflection aren't strong enough to overturn the ruling, but I have not
seen LSJ explain why he believes the 1999 ruling is best for the game.
Why shouldn't a Deflection attempt be possible before or after or
between blocking attempts if the target meth has not stated that he or
she chooses not to block or implied same by one of the more universally
established means? I'm more than willing to accept that LSJ sees the
implications of the ruling much more clearly than I. Maybe it has near
and/or far reaching effects that avoid other conflicts. He has done a
good job of clarifying the ruling, and explaining how play goes under
it, but I and others on this thread want to know the rationale behind
it. Is that too much to ask?

But there is specific text on Mask stating that the action resumes
where it left off. After resolution the action is over, so there's no
action to resume. That's what I would point out as the reason to
disallow it, anyway. Deflection has no such text. I see where you are
going though, see below.

> While there's nothing explicitly on Deflection that would keep it from being
> playable when Enhanced Senses is, it can't be. Something to do with its function.

I'm not crazy about this comparison either, because Enhanced Senses is
played after the intent to block is announced and during a block
attempt. I think we agree that Deflection in the middle of a block
attempt would be bad for the game. Maybe this is more a criticism of
6.2's statement that a reaction card can be played at "any" time during
an action rather than justification for disallowing play of Deflection
before, after or between individual block attempts.

> You can't have one of your minions try to "send it on" without inherently having
> decided not block it yourself.

Ah there's the rub for me. I was thinking of a Deflection reaction as
something akin to or conceptually the same as a block. I was focusing
on the similarities, and that's a valid point about the differences. A
successful block attempt causes the action to become unsuccessful,
while a successful deflection attempt certainly does not. Fair enough.

Someone may have already asked in this thread. Would this also apply
to all of the reaction cards that reduce bleeds and don't have specific
text starting with "only usable...?" Cards like Confusion of the Eye or
Ecstasy at basic. If so, would that mean that a non-target meth could
only play Folderol at superior if the target meth had already declined
to block explicitly or implicitly? All of the other reaction cards i
can think of either provide intercept like Enhanced Senses (implying
that they can only be used during a block attempt), or have specific
text that removes any ambiguity i can think of.

I think that's would be a much fairer statement than the one Jeroen is
offering. If that's what it boils down to, fine. But let's call the issue
what it is: a dislike for DI because it breaks up combos and he thinks the
game ought to reward the successful use of card combinations better than it
now does. Don't conjure some "flaw" out of thin air and use that to justify
your desire to tinker with the game. Because if you do, other people can
then use your argument to attack other cards in all sorts of unpredictable
ways. If that a card is unique or highly broad or can be shown to have a
low requirement threshold becomes a justification for it becoming banned,
there will be no end to the number of card ban threads based on the same
reasoning.

Fred

(except intercept and Cat's Guidance, which already have defined timing
windows)? Wouldn't it be better for the game if reactions all follow
the same rules of play timing (except intercept, etc...as defined
above)?

Example of consistency:
Player A: Frederick the Weak bleeds for 1.
Player B: Gilbert Duane ATTEMPTS to reduce the bleed by 2.
Player C: I Direct Intervention the bleed reduction card.
Player B: Well, then Gilbert attempts to block.

Player A: Frederick the Weak bleeds for 1.
Player B: Gilbert Duane ATTEMPTS to deflect the bleed to C.
Player C: I Direct Intervention the bleed bounce card.
Player B: Well, then Gilbert attempts to block.

Situation 2 under the current ruling:

Player A: Frederick the Weak bleeds for 1.
Player B: Gilbert Duane ATTEMPTS to deflect the bleed to C.
Player C: I Direct Intervention the bleed bounce card.
Player B: Well, I guess I have to take it since I can't block (cause
LSJ said so).

As opposed to the recent text change to bounce cards, did you ever
consider adding text that prohibits them from being played during a
currently succeeding block attempt? Please explain your reasoning
either way.

;-)

> > We'll have to agree to disagree on the commonality of pitching a pool,
> > since neither of us has statics to back up his viewpoint.
>
> Exactly. Thanks for selling it to the cheap seats, though.

Hey, I wasn't the one who introduced the concept of an "implict
no-block" which set the foundation for a plethora of bad rulings based
upon this precedent. The very idea that you can anounce an intention
not to block without actually saying "I don't block" sets a precedent
that the acting player can deny the reacting player the capacity to
block without card play.

> >> Commonly, the majority playgroups play it properly, as an implicit declination
> >> of blocking, which it is (or as explicitly stated).
> >>
> >> There is nothing to be gained, except aiding cheating, by allowing it to "draw
> >> out" a modifier that the acting player doesn't intend to play until after blocks
> >> are declined.
> >
> > Then obviously the acting player has the ability to ask, "Do you
> > block?" even after the pool has been pitched.
>
> Pointlessly, since the question has already been answered (the defending player
> cannot expect to reach the pitching pool stage unless he has declined to block;
> since it was the defending player's impulse (his turn in sequence to play the
> next effect), his options were: "so-and-so plays a reaction", "I play a master:
> out-of-turn", "so-an-so blocks", or "no block". That is the exhaustive list of
> his choices at his impulse. Which of those choices is indicated by pitching a
> pool? The "no block" one, of course).

And yet, he still has not been asked if he blocks, and still has not
answered that he doesn't block. There is no fundamental difference
between playing a reaction card and blocking after the acting player
plays an action modifier. The play of the action modifier makes the
pitching of a pool a misplay, therefore the pool is retracted and play
is rewound.

> > Nothing is stopping the
> > acting player from asking, "Do you block?"
>
> Nothing is stopping him from asking "is it my turn?" either, but both are obvious.

Your rhetorical statement misses the point. Can the defending player
deny the acting player his turn?

> > Even in the rulebook it states that this is an "event".
> > You can't go skipping events.
>
> Correct. At the defending player's impulse, though, he declined to react or
> block, so it must be the case that he declined to block.

Yes, he issued no response to either reacting or blocking.

By that same logic, you haven't responded to the accusation that you
are haven't stopped beating your wife. So you must be a wife beater.

Obviously, the previous statement was fictiious and I have no evidence
to support the accusation of spousal abuse (cuz we all know your wife
would kick your ass. :P). What it shows is that in fact your implied
declined to block in the absense of someone asking "Do you block?" is
non-sensical. You can not implicitly respond to a question that hasn't
been asked.

> Nothing was skipped. (And it is now the acting player's impulse, since "no
> block" is an event, so he may play bleed boosters).

The "event" of "no block" was never addressed. You may say it was
addressed but it wasn't. It was skipped. It was skipped by the acting
player who never prompted for a response to the "event".

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr
XZealot
Archon of the Swamp

Here's the problem, James. You can't decline to block implicitly as it
is an explicitly written in the rules that you must declare whether you
are blocking or not. If their is a misplay then the play backs up to
the point where the misplay can be resolved.

Let me lay it out for you. The various stage of an action are as
follows.

A) action is announced
B) Action modifiers are played
C) Reactions are played
D) Block attempts are declared
E) Action Modifiers are played
F) Reactions are played
G) Combat ensues from a successful block.
H) If blocking minion fails, then other block attempts are solicited.
I) Barring another minion successfully blocking
1) You decline to block
2) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to block
3) The acting Methuselah declines to play modifiers
4) You decline to play reactions
5) All other non-acting Meths (cw) decline to play reactions
6) You pitch a pool into the bank

Since the pool was pitched and the reacting player never declined to
block the play reverts to step B for this misplay.

No, it's not.

There is one example in the rules where the player explicitly asks "Do
you block?", and the player decides not to. This is perfectly
reasonable play, by the way. Note: the example does not say how they
communicate it. It could be "No, I don't block." It could be "Bah,
tapped out." It could be a shake of the head, a wave of the hand from
side to side indicating "No" while they choke on a cookie.

Similarly reasonable play would be for the acting Methuselah to play
Govern the Unaligned, draw a replacement, play Seduction, draw a
replacement, play The Sleeping Mind, draw a replacement, look at their
hand, and say "That's it." The reacting Methuselah looks at his hand,
starts picking up pool, asks how much the bleed is for... 3, no 4
because of Anneke's built in +1 bleed. The reacting Methuselah throws 4
pool into the blood bank. All done. Everything's been communicated.
No-one is confused.

The rules do not specify or enforce the manner in which players must
communicate. As another example, it is notable that one common reaction
to Madness of the Bard being played was for players to communicate non-
verbally to limit the amount of speaking they had to do - such as
shaking their head, pointing at vampires, and so on. This was similarly
legal play.

I am not sure where you have extracted this idea that players do not
develop short-hand or that the rules require every possible step to be
announced at all points. They don't. If the players understand what's
going on, that's fine. If a step is rushed by by accident, back up.

This isn't hard.

resources for that particular type of cost in abundance.

Example:

- I have to tap two untapped minions to cancel one minion's action.

two minions untapped, to stop one action. However, in a breed
deck, I might have spare minions a-plenty.

particular type of action, say), but very common (a bleed), flexibility
isn't so hot. I don't need the flexibility because I reckon I'm very
likely to see that situation in play on a very regular basis. At which
point I don't need such a large level of flexibility, because I'm
picking on something that happens all the time.

asked to. In the official rulebook! Even though they have to be asked
to! OH NOES!

You. Are. Wrong.

Note also that the rulebook doesn't specify what language players have
to use, nor does it specify that all players must use a mutually
comprehensible language, nor does it specify (in fact) whether or not
players are allowed to talk save for the examples of text (which are
clearly exceptions from the general silence and pointing), and so on.

I can also show you dozens of rulings from LSJ that show that this is
legal play, so long as players understand what is going on. Those are
statements of the official position, whether in the rulebook or not.
Some things don't end up in there, because they're considered obvious.

>>If the players understand what's
>> going on, that's fine. If a step is rushed by by accident, back up.
>
>As soon as you deny a player the opportunity to announce his/her block
>then you need to back up to where they can decide whether to block or
>not.

The player is not denied a chance to block. If they want to block, they
announce an attempt to block. If they decline to block, they don't get
an attempt.

The acting Methuselah cannot deny them that chance - unless they have
some particular card effect, of course, that would take out their
blocker(s). It's just that if the reacting Methuselah voluntarily does
things that imply they're not blocking (like saying "I'm not blocking"
or paying the pool for a bleed), they've declared they're not blocking.
Similarly, the acting Methuselah asking his grand-prey "Hands for one?"
does not deny the grand-prey the chance to maneuver or play pre-range
cards, even if the acting Methuselah is trying to indicate his
willingness to skip ahead to Choose Strike.

The situation here is entirely that voluntary action from the reacting
Methuselah indicates something that they want to do (or don't want to
do), even if they don't use a specific, Norm-defined incantation to
indicate it.

This is so completely unlike the acting Methuselah being able to deny
other player the opportunity to do things - because it's those other
players who are voluntarily giving up the chance to do those things by
indicating somehow that they don't want to block - that I can only
imagine you have completely taken leave of your senses.

Incorrect.

At his turn in the sequence, the sequencing rules themselves put him up to it
(the sequencing is, in essense, asking him the question: "do you react or
initiate a block attempt?").

His response at that impulse is "pitch a pool".

This response cannot be misconstrued as "I intend to play a reaction"
nor can it be misconstrued as "I intend to have a minion attempt to block".

It can only be construed as "I do not attempt to react or block at this time".

The "at this time" is not "sticky" for reactions -- he can react again later at
his next impulse.

The "at this time" is "sticky" for blocking, however. The decision not to block
is final.

sequencing dictates that it is A's turn to play an effect or pass.

sequencing dictates that it is B's turn to play an effect or pass.
silence
silence
silence

a misplay, since it was indeed the defending Methuselah's impulse.

Rewinding to before the decision not to block is not necessary, since making
that decision was not a misplay and, moreover, rewinding to that point would be
actively wrong because rewinding to that point would *obviously* be giving an
advantage to the player making the misplay.

Gaining an advantage from misplays is improper.

Intentionally doing to is cheating.

Arguing in favor of allowing intentionally gaining an advantage through such
play, well, doesn't look good.

Either that or he made no decision and cheated by pitching in a pool.

Either way, he is not to be given an advantage after pitching a pool and waiting

shadow of a parallel from which to draw any insight to the current question of

There is no sequencing rule that requires me to react or make a declaration no
"stop beating".

>> Nothing was skipped. (And it is now the acting player's impulse, since "no
>> block" is an event, so he may play bleed boosters).
>

Messages.Author: J. Hunter Johnson
Messages.Body:
XZealot wrote:
> You can't decline to block implicitly as it is an explicitly
> written in the rules that you must declare whether you
> are blocking or not.

And you can follow the explicit rule by making that declaration through
an action such as pitching in a pool.

That declaration does *not* resolve the action. It does serve to speed
up cases where no other action modifiers are going to be played before
resolution though.

You cannot skip the acting player's chance to play action modifiers by
pitching in a pool. If you declare "no block" by pitching in a pool
and then discover that the offered shortcut through resolution is not
taken, you back up to the point where the not-you player would like to
insert her legitimate action modifier. That is, you have declined to
block but haven't yet lost the pool.

The reasons (keep the defender from gleaning extra information before a
block declaration, keep the penalty for intentional attempts to do so
on the correct party) have been explained.

If this interpretation does not fit how you've been (mis)playing it,
adjust your play, but don't ask for permission for players to cheat.

players share this opinion. I think that's very unlikely in the case of

>> into the game" and every time you try to articulate your basis, it keeps
>> coming down to, "DI does something other cards don't do".
>
>1. I have as much basis to say it don't fit as you have to say it does fit.

Not really.

1) If Direct Intervention doesn't fit, what has it been doing in the
game in the 10 years since it was first printed?

It seems pretty likely that if D.I. really didn't fit, it would have to
have had a plethora of changes made to it to make it fit. Which,
actually, it hasn't. It's been a remarkably stable card. Certainly,
there has been the need for certain clarifications - such as what
happens if I D.I. Threats, can I still play Conditioning? - but the
basic card hasn't really changed.

That a card may be confusing and players may need some guidance from
time to time doesn't mean it doesn't fit. Obvious other examples of
such cards are Madness Network and Mask of a Thousand Faces, or
Banishment back when it was first printed. Confusing in their own way,
and yet no-one would really say that they didn't fit in the game.

2) It's possible that Direct Intervention was an effect completely out
of left-field when it was printed, but does it fit now?

This possibility may have legs. The basic set, Jyhad/V:TES, is a big
set, but is having to set all the possibilities for the game. Dark
Sovereigns and Ancient Hearts are, largely, dominated by the Indies.
And then we get Sabbat, which is sort of a base set, sort of a new set.
So it's possible at that point that D.I. could have been said to not fit
- but much in the same way that Corruption could be said to not fit,
because it was one card that did this really weird thing oddly. And yet
Corruption is clearly a core Setite ability, and has been expanded on in
the sets since.

Perhaps then, D.I. is a new thing for cards to do when it's printed, but
has been expanded on since.

Actually, it has.

Example: Louhi, in Kindred Most Wanted.
Once each turn, if Louhi is ready, she may burn 1 blood to
cancel an action card played by a vampire controlled by your
predator as it is played (the acting minion doesn't tap).

So that's a pretty versatile cancellation. Not as versatile as D.I.,
but cheaper. (Potentially, usable more than once per turn round the
table, if the predator does something freakish with OOT actions, too.)

Still, we're not quite as versatile as D.I., and it may be that massive
versatility that means it doesn't fit. Except we do have that massive
versatility available:

Khalu may burn 5 blood to cancel a minion card played by your
predator or prey as it is played (no cost is paid).

So are we to say that Louhi doesn't fit, and Khalu doesn't fit? Note
that Khalu can even burn 5 blood during my turn - EVEN MORE powerful
than DI. Load up on blood gain, and we're away.

We've also seen a very versatile defence for the Imbued, in the form of
React with Conviction, the ability to defend themselves against actions
or strikes. We've had Approximation of Loyalty give you the ability to
scoop out Wakes, intercept, bounce etc. from your prey and screw things
over.

This wide-ranging cancellation thing seems to fit now, because it's been
developed interestingly.

3) And really, did D.I. come out of nowhere?

Not really. Sudden Reversal was a counter-spell for masters. Watenda
could take out combat cards he didn't like. It's not like D.I. actually
came from nowhere. Delaying Tactics didn't kill a specific card, but
could certainly have much the same effect - not the political card (that
goes back to your hand, obviously), but the other effects that were
played, such as letting a player play their vote-push, then cancelling
the vote, so you've basically just "cancelled" all the vote push cards.
(See also Business Pressure and Telepathic Vote Counting.)

That sort of effect was out there.

4) So, does D.I. cross some line where cards aren't supposed to go?

Not really. Master cards can affect minions, that's pretty well
established - Rotschreck is probably the best-known example from Jyhad,
but also Elysium: The Arboretum, for example. It's perfectly possible
for master cards to affect minions, either directly (play now, resolve
now) or less directly (play now, use later). Other examples: Frenzy,
Mob Connections, Police Department.

And we've had all sorts of bizarre interactions since then. Rewind Time
(a minion card) can cancel master cards as they're being played.
Regarhagan's Hold, a master card, can actually prevent certain reaction
cards being played. Angel of Berlin is an M:OOT that untaps minions.
Minion cards (e.g. all of Abombwe, Tranquility) can cancel Frenzy cards
of any sort, be they minion or master.

It's pretty clear that different areas of the game (such as card types)
can interact in unusual ways, and have always been able to.

5) So is it out of line thematically?

Seems unlikely. Quite a bit of White Wolf source material has
Methuselahs and even, in some cases, Antediluvians being personally
involved - though often obscurely - in the Jyhad. Though obviously it's
much better for them if they can achieve all their aims through proxies,
to keep their fingerprints off their schemes, there's never been an
active prohibition towards doing things that might be questionable or a
little risky. Direct Intervention could certainly fit into that sort of
action. After all, you're paying pool and screwing your ability to play
Dreams of the Sphinx next turn.

I'm really not sure how you can argue that the effect doesn't fit in the
game. It may (or may not) be inappropriately costed, but the effect
seems a fairly integral part of V:TES as it stands at the end of 2006.



>

There's all sorts of cards in the game which aren't dependent on combinations.
Or they're not so dependent that it matters a great deal whether one part of
them gets canceled.

Another thing you can do is to play with an abundance of the combo-worthy
cards. So if you get one Wolf Claws canceled (for example), you're quite
likely to have another in hand - making all the costs, the pool, the MPA,
the time spent holding the DI all pointless. I think this tends to be
the big downside of DI, especially given that your opponent usually can't
see your hand and never knows what's in your deck (unless you play the
same deck over and over in the same playgroup).

> Is Govern+lost in Crowds + Elder Impersonation + Conditioning + Scouting mission a combo that is way too long?
> DI wreaks havoc on every step of that combo.

You don't necessarily need the entire combo. Especially if you have a
profuse collection of different stealth cards and bleed enhancers so you
don't run afoul of rule against playing the same action modifier twice in
a given action. That rule aside, this combo is rife with opportunity to
replace any particular piece which gets DIed, screwing the player who
tried to employ it. In fact, I seldom see DIs used against stealth/bleed
combinations and I suspect this is the reason.

> If your prey flicks, and you play Scouting Mission,

(I'm going to assume you meant Spying Mission, not Scouting Mission)

> and he plays the DI on the scouting mission you have effectively wasted 1 action + 3 blood for a bleed of 6 on your grand
> predator.

As with everything, you can always advance some situation or other where the
card being disputed looks totally awesome. Whether that situation is a
truly common enough to make the point convincing or not is what's easy
to dispute. Sure, you can use DI to counter a Spying Mission and you've
made a great play. Great work if you can get it.

Don't ask me. I didn't think it did. It never seemed to be bad where
I played. But a lot of people were complaining about it and it got
banned. I do not believe, nor did I eversee any explanation of it from
VEKN, that it was banned because it gave a player too much power to
throw victory to _other_ players as opposed to himself.

>> What does "the controller of the (having) too much power over the
>> game" mean - if not power to get ousts? And particularly, what does
>> it mean that anyone would care about?
>
> So a card that would say: you cannot be ousted until after 10 turns would not be broken because it doesn't give you power to oust?

Sure it gives you the power to oust. Since you wouldn't have to concentrate
on defense at that point, you could shift all of your resources to offense
and this would make it much more likely that you could get ousts.

>>>> No. I'm saying the words just above your quote.
>>>>
>>>> I will repeat: Lots of people win without packing a DI. That means it's
>>>> not "broken" or "overpowered" or anything along those lines. I believe
>>>> you have some problem with it, but it's very unclear to me because you

>>

>> Club granting a player power "over" the game - whatever that means.

Maybe mull over in your head that whatever you think you've explained hasn't
been expressed very well. Players having the 'power' to throw the game to
other players, as you've suggested is your meaning vis-a-vis Succubus Club
is: 1) inherent in the game and already addressed by the play-to-win rule;
2) certainly not a common problem in any case; and 3) is not and was never
your complaint about DI as far as I can see. This makes it seem like the
reference was ad hoc definition of the term you produced just because someone
cornered you and demanded to know what you're talking about, if not
brokeness. These are the things I mull over in my head when you say shit
like this.

>>>>> Maybe that
>>>>> you think the 1 pool cost makes up for the playability it gains versus
>>>>> SR. I certainly don't.
>>>>
>>>> I certainly do, yes. I think you're underestimating this cost. I also
>>>> think you're overestimating its utility.
>>>
>>> you said yourself you don't see the card that much. I'm not estimating anything. I see it in action every game I play.
>>
>> I'm using the word 'estimate' to mean 'reckon' or 'summarize'. This has
>> nothing to with how often one sees a card.
>
> No, but my complaint is based on how much I see the card. See the difference?

brokeness, I disagree. There may be all sorts of reasons having nothing to
do with the overall utility of Direct Intervention why your group (and
David Cherryholmes group, apparently) sees the card more often than I do and,
I believe, in most places.

>>I suspect you're mainly frustrated
>> that it won't allow you to use the strategies you want to use in order to
>> win games. Not that it's too powerful, in any sense.
>
> 1. I'm not frustrated. Certainly not about strategies I want to use. That's what you misread in a comment that was tongue in
> cheek. You seem obsessed by the combo thing. You haven't even shown me how you play without comboing cards.

I think the explanation above demonstrates my response to that. It's not
so much that I don't play with comboing cards on some level. It's just that
DI frequently doesn't work against it or doesn't work well enough to justify
its costs.

> 2. If a single card should dictate how you play the game, it really is overpowered.

Not necessarily. Any staple card, like Blood Doll, Wake with Evening's
Freshness, Govern, Conditioning, and so forth will have effects on the game
which people have to take into account when building and playing decks. The
"single card" thing seems to your problem, not a real problem. I don't see
how it makes a difference whether the card is unique in it's particular
effect or not. If they added a card:

Callous Intervention
Master Out-of-Turn
Burn two blood from any single vampire you control or burn one blood from any
two vampires you control. If you do, Cancel a minion card as it is played.
No cost is paid. (If it was an action card, the acting minion doesn't tap.
If it was a strike card, the minion chooses another strike.)

Would adding this card make Direct Intervention acceptable to you? If not,
why not, considering that your one of your stated problems with the card is its
uniqueness? How does it matter whether there's one card or two separate cards
that do approximately the same thing in the game?

> 3. The game effect of a lot of DI is that the decks with the most recursion of cards win. Is that a needed effect?

I don't know that any effect in the game is needed. The issue is whether it's
bad - and if so, why is it bad? Is it necessarily bad that the existence of
DI helps decks using recursions of cards?

Fred
