Messages.Body:
> Now, what effect (or pass) is indicated by "pitch a pool".
>
> To a reasonable player, that is?

Since I obviously have the appearance of being unreasonably
arguementative about this point, I will bite.

The effect indicated by "pitch a pool" is that the action resolves for
a loss of 1 pool by the defending player.

> > There is no fundamental difference
> > between playing a reaction card and blocking after the acting player
> > plays an action modifier. The play of the action modifier makes the
> > pitching of a pool a misplay, therefore the pool is retracted and play
> > is rewound.
>
> Correct. Rewound to the point of the misplay, and rewound so that the player
> making the misplay gains no advantage.
>
> The misplay was skipping the acting Meth's impulse (his window to play a
> modifier after the "no block" decision). The "no block" decision itself was not
> a misplay, since it was indeed the defending Methuselah's impulse.
>
> Rewinding to before the decision not to block is not necessary, since making
> that decision was not a misplay and, moreover, rewinding to that point would be
> actively wrong because rewinding to that point would *obviously* be giving an
> advantage to the player making the misplay.

Or, it would prompt the acting player to queue the question, "Do you
block?" into his action sequence before playing his action modifier.

>Rewinding to before the decision not to block is not necessary, since making that >decision was not a misplay and, moreover, rewinding to that point would be actively wrong >because rewinding to that point would *obviously* be giving an advantage to the player >making the misplay,

Since you are rewinding the action back prior to before the action
resolves and you are allowing the action to be modified by an action
modifier, why is it not within the blocking player's ability to block,
when they have not explicitly declared "no block". The only wrongness
commited here is that the acting player did not request any block
attempts. You cannot imply something that hasn't occured, or will not
occur, especially once you rewind play back to before the possibility
of the event occuring.

> Gaining an advantage from misplays is improper.

The sequence of the action is thrown off by an action modifier being
played on a action that has resolved. There are two misplays occuring.
One by the acting player by not requesting any block attempts who then
plays an action modifier on a resolved action. The other is the
defending player pitching a pool prematurely. Both players are
participating in the misplay. Both are attempting to gain an improper
advantage from that misplay.

> Intentionally doing to is cheating.
>
> Arguing in favor of allowing intentionally gaining an advantage through such
> play, well, doesn't look good.

Absolutely, that is why I think that this ruling that the acting player
gets to cheat by playing an action modifier on a resolved action by
implying that there is a block decline looks as poor for you as me
arguing that this ruling is in error by allowing the defending player
to attempt to block after the acting player believes that there was an
implied decline to block.

The best ruling would be that during each action, that it should be
manditory that all methuselah's legally able to declare a "no block" if
they are not attempting to block (Eagle Sight and Falcon's Eye would
still retain their suprise value). This is fundamentally in the spirit
of the game. To do otherwise is a misplay.

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr
XZealot

Archon of the Swamp (except when my wife is around and then she gets to
wear the title)

Messages.Body:
(Again, note "Subject:" change.)

In message <1166547315....@n67g2000cwd.googlegroups.com>,

Jeroen <joen...@hotmail.com> writes:
>Fuzzy logic. Because that would mean all defensive card can be more
>powerful than the offensive cards. A lot of cards were banned or
>changed without being a problem as you just defined 'being a problem'

Actually, a lot of the best defensive cards are more powerful than
similar offensive cards.

For example: assume I'm playing a bleed deck. I want to bleed you for
six. So, I'm playing Ozmo (AUS dom obf +1 bleed). I throw down Govern
the Unaligned, so we're at four bleed, for one blood.

So far, you have paid with one card from your hand, 1 blood if/when the
action is successful, and you've "paid" for Ozmo having +1 bleed, and
such.

Now I declare a block, hoping, praying that you don't have any stealth
in hand. (This may be a tactical error on my part.) You look through
your hand and play Faceless Night, or any other Obfuscate modifier of
your choice for +1 stealth.

At this point, I can't block. So you now play Conditioning. Bang, six
bleed.

So, 6 bleed, 3 cards from hand, +1 stealth, 1 blood, and 1 blood when
successful, plus the cost of Ozmo.

Now, how do I get my prey bled for me for 6 at +1 stealth?

I play one card, for one blood, with a 2 cap vampire - Dominate bounce.
Or if I happen to have superior Dominate, I could play Redirection and
make it free, or stay untapped with Deflection.

One card, one small vampire, and maybe one blood has got a great deal of
damage (possibly) done to my prey. You had to play several cards to
attempt the same.

What's the difference here? Opportunity cost. I have to hold my
defence until it's playable and, as a result, will often include less of
it in my deck than you can include offensive cards. (Some easily cycled
or burn option cards would be mild exceptions here.) I can't control
when I get to play them, and I don't get to choose that you do things
that actively help me.

Note that the threat of defensive cards can also cause you problems.
You know I have some bounce in my deck, but looking over my ash-heap of,
say, 40 cards out of what looks like an 80-90 deck, you can see 3. Do I
have 6 in the deck? Do I have one in hand? Do you want to play stealth
to get by me, do you want to suffer the block, do you want to jam your
hand for now? Fun fun fun.

But when I do get to play it, I can often take a powerful situation and
use it to my significant advantage. But I don't get to control the
situation - I just have to hope that bleed will be a significant issue
on the tables I'm on, which is usually a reasonable bet.

Compare other similarly popular cards in defensive roles:

- Delaying Tactics can not only nullify a vote right now (which would be
a pretty even trade), it can also prevent anyone else you
control from calling it for the rest of the turn, which is an
uneven trade. The cost? What happens if no-one calls a vote
you want to stop?

- You come rushing me (requiring a card or a fairly expensive built-in
action), throw down a couple of combat cards (perhaps Carrion
Crows and Scorpion Sting)... I play Majesty. Three cards
nullified by 1 card. I don't know that I'm going to get rushed,
but it works out well.

But it gets even better. I act. Get blocked. You might waste
resources on blocking me, and might try to hit me. And not only
can I get away from your fiendish Combat of Doom, I can untap,
leave your minion tapped, and act again. But no use at all if I
don't get blocked or rushed. But bloody useful when I do.

Now, of course, there are defensive cards that are a Festering Pile of
Wank (see Eyes of the Dead). But look at the ones that see regular
play, see how one card can nullify several, see how one card can give
you a serious advantage - but see how the opportunity cost goes up, so
the power/cost ratio is hopefully balanced.

The good offensive cards, I can usually control a lot more, and so their
opportunity cost is significantly lower, and since they have that sort
of lower cost, their individual power is often lower, or their other
costs are non-trivially higher.

In the ideal, anyway - no-one's going to deny there aren't exceptions
(good and bad) in both arenas.

definitions.

I did say that Direct Intervention is out of character in a given way,
and I don't think you're going to find any good counterexamples to it.
I mean, you might find other effects also out of character to the game
of VTES as a whole. But probably not out of character in the same way,
or to the same degree, as DI is.

As you say - and I said - out of character doesn't necessarily mean
bad. But if you like the overall character of a game, you may not like
elements of the game (whether added to the game later on, as DI was, or
not) that don't fit that character.

The current designers apparently disagree. While there aren't a metric
assload of such effects, not only have they not altered Direct
Intervention, they've printed Khalu who is even broader in effect - no
restrictions on timing here, unlike a M:OoT (which is only usable OoT).

Khalu is, of course, pretty expensive. But expense isn't an element to
consider when the object of consideration is, as you stated in your
earlier post:

>>I think it's clear that the game was not
>> built on broad, general effects, but on small, narrow effects.

So it's an expensive but broad, general effect.

Similarly, Louhi who can cancel every action, equipment, retainer, ally,
or political action card in the game, when played by your predator.
Which seems pretty broad to me.

The current designers seem quite happy letting people have broad,
general effects as well as small, narrow effects. The *good* small,
narrow effects are often better, of course - cheaper, easier to play,
using the effect against itself not just cancelling it, potentially
effective against cardless or permanent actions etc.

> succeeds, the acting Meth declares the block successful and you go directly
> to combat (or effects playable "when a block succeeds"). General effects
> (like bleed reduction) aren't supposed to be usable. See LSJ 8-May-2005:
>

Ah. Right.

Chris had a good point in that, though, in that the equating of a pass from the
acting Methuselah in response to sufficient intercept as the event of
"successful block", the sequencing order gets jarred in what could be an
unintuitive manner.

But it suffices - the acting Methuselah cannot "pass" when being successfully
blocked. She can only activate an effect (like more stealth, some random effect
hoping to top-deck stealth or just cycle cards, or, if no other effect, then
then "effect" of making the block successful).

Once successful, the action enters resolution, where most reaction cards cannot
be played.

You can play Telepathic Counter during a block attempt window, however (unlike
Deflection), which is more closely related to the thread, if not the immediate
question :-).

Eh? Kind of arrogant about that, sounds like to me. (You are such a well-
known shit-talker! :-) ) I think we'll have to disagree about that part.
My main point, though, was not so much about who's right and who's wrong.
I'm just trying to point out that all this stuff about DI being overbroad
in its utility lacks any means of making a distinction between cards that
are too broad and those that aren't. In short, how did you draw that line?

> I was trying to write about the game of VTES as a whole. You know, the
> big picture. Obviously you don't see the same big picture that I do.

Oh, I think when push comes to shove, I can see how DI is "special". But
it sort of seems to me that it's all in what you're looking for. If
someone wants to make an argument that DI shouldn't exist, this is an
easy distinction to reach for - but it strikes as a pretty subjective one
in the end. Likewise, if I want to say it's just fine, it's pretty easy
to be pig-stubborn and say it's really no different. The argument about
DI being OK or bad really ought to hinge on something distinct that it
does that's bad - unless you can prove that it's overpowered (probably
requiring backup from the TWDA). If you want to say, "It's bad because
it breaks up combinations and the game is more fun when it encourages
effective use of card combinations", that's a sort of point to which I'm
much more sympathetic. (But it's harder to get the powers that be to
take action on such a complaint.)

> I did say that Direct Intervention is out of character in a given way,
> and I don't think you're going to find any good counterexamples to it.

I don't see how anyone could find counterexamples to such a claim. Like
saying, "Prove to me with counterexamples how PTO is not overpowered."

> I mean, you might find other effects also out of character to the game
> of VTES as a whole. But probably not out of character in the same way,
> or to the same degree, as DI is.

Sure. That is the nature of an effect being out of character. If I
could, you'd have never made the claim in the first place. But that
was never my point. At least, I can find other cards that are out of
character to the game and claim it's to the same degree - given that
there's no metric for measuring out-of-characterness. And since the
reasoning was that DI was only "DI is too out-of-character thus it's
bad", it's easy to suggest alternative cards that are likewise out-
of-character. It's impossible to prove the two situations are
comparable - but it's likewise impossible to disprove as well.

> As you say - and I said - out of character doesn't necessarily mean
> bad. But if you like the overall character of a game, you may not like
> elements of the game (whether added to the game later on, as DI was, or
> not) that don't fit that character.

Sure.

Fred
